title: Five elements of financial statements and recognition
duplicates: college:study material/THAPAR MBA/THAPAR MBA/FINANCIAL ACCOUNTINGAND REPORTING/Five Elements_FS_Recognition.pdf

slides.visual_text: A page from the Conceptual Framework (source: a link to the Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting PDF on ifrs.org), section Introduction. Paragraph 4.1 splits the elements into two groups: assets, liabilities and equity relate to financial position; income and expenses relate to financial performance. Paragraph 4.2 says the elements link to the economic resources, claims and changes in them discussed in Chapter 1, and points to Table 4.1. Table 4.1, The elements of financial statements, has three columns: the item from Chapter 1, the element, and its definition. Economic resource maps to Asset (a present economic resource the entity controls because of past events; an economic resource is a right that can produce economic benefits). Claim maps to Liability (a present obligation to transfer an economic resource because of past events) and Equity (what is left of the assets after deducting all liabilities, the residual interest). Changes reflecting financial performance map to Income (asset increases or liability decreases that raise equity, excluding contributions from equity holders) and Expenses (asset decreases or liability increases that lower equity, excluding distributions to equity holders). Other changes have no element: contributions from and distributions to equity holders, and exchanges of assets or liabilities that leave equity unchanged.

A page from the Conceptual Framework headed The recognition process, paragraphs 5.1 to 5.4. 5.1 defines recognition: capturing an item that meets the definition of an element (asset, liability, equity, income or expenses) for inclusion in the statement of financial position or the statement(s) of financial performance, by showing it in words and a monetary amount and including that amount in the statement's totals; the amount at which an asset, liability or equity is recognised is its carrying amount. 5.2 says these statements are structured summaries meant to make information comparable and understandable, and recognised amounts feed the totals and subtotals. 5.3 (pointing to Diagram 5.1) links the elements and statements: at the start and end of the period, total assets minus total liabilities equal total equity; recognised changes in equity are income minus expenses, plus contributions from equity holders minus distributions to them. 5.4 says the statements are linked because recognising one item needs the recognition or derecognition of another: income is recognised together with a new or larger asset, or a removed or smaller liability; expenses are recognised together with a new or larger liability, or a removed or smaller asset.

A page from the Conceptual Framework. Diagram 5.1, How recognition links the elements of financial statements: four stacked boxes joined by plus and equals signs. Box one, statement of financial position at the beginning of the reporting period (assets minus liabilities equal equity), plus box two, statement(s) of financial performance (income minus expenses), plus box three (contributions from holders of equity claims minus distributions to them), equals box four, statement of financial position at the end of the reporting period (assets minus liabilities equal equity). A bracket groups boxes two and three as Changes in equity. Below, paragraph 5.5: when assets or liabilities are first recognised, income and related expenses can be recognised at the same time. Its example is a sale of goods for cash: income comes from recognising one asset (the cash) and an expense from derecognising another asset (the goods sold). This simultaneous recognition is sometimes called the matching of costs with income. The Conceptual Framework leads to matching when it comes from recognising changes in assets and liabilities, but matching is not one of its objectives, and it does not allow items that fail the definition of an asset, a liability or equity onto the statement of financial position.
